newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli cabinet agrees to West Bank pullback.
newsitem.headline: Israeli cabinet agrees to West Bank pullback.

text.p: Israel's cabinet on Friday approved a further troop withdrawal in the West Bank, a move that could ease tensions with the Palestinians but strain the ruling coalition.

After a seven-hour debate, the cabinet voted 10-7 to back a proposal by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to hand over another nine percent of the West Bank to the Palestinians, said a government spokeswoman.
Two percent of the area to be handed over comprises territory that is fully under Israeli control.

The withdrawal, which Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said would take at least 48 hours to implement, would be the first of three from mainly rural areas of the West Bank, with the last to be completed by mid-1998.
Final borders are to be decided in permanent status talks scheduled to begin this month.

"The government has empowered the prime minister, the defence minister and the foreign minister to announce to the Palestinian Authority the formula for further redeployment and to coordinate its implementation," said a government statement.
Israel television said Netanyahu had been under U.S, pressure to placate the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) after approving new Jewish housing in Arab East Jeruslem.
Netanyahu, a right-winger elected nine months ago on a promise to get tough in talks with the Palestinians, was bound by an agreement reached in January to relinquish more West Bank land by Friday.

But the move could strain his ruling coalition. Three legislators from parties belonging to the coalition threatened publicly to stop supporting the government in parliament if the pullback was too deep.

"I don't see myself as part of the coalition which hands over voluntarily parts of the Land of Israel without having been asked to do so," said Moshe Peled of the nationalist Tsomet party. Israel television said before the government decision that at least seven of the 18 cabinet members believed an offer of nine percent of territory would be too generous.

The government commands 66 seats in the 120-member parliament but dissenting voices inside the coalition have become stronger since Netanyahu's handover in January of most of the West Bank town of Hebron.

Israel has handed over only about three percent of West Bank land to Palestinian self-rule since its landmark 1993 peace deal with the PLO, but the territory Israel left contains eight major Arab towns. Israel has also given the PLO civil control in some 450 villages.
Palestinians in the West Bank town of Halhoul, near Hebron, prepared for the end of 30 years of military occupation.
Halhul residents decorated their town with Palestinian flags and pictures of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and painted storefronts.
"We are going to be free. We will not see Israeli soldiers anymore," said Ashraf Ali Milhem, 15.
In East Jerusalem, a Palestinian lawyer said he would meet Israeli police to discuss their official warning to four Palestinian offices to close by Sunday or be shut.
"We agreed on a meeting for Sunday," Jawad Boulos said. "If we fail to come to conclusions, I will prepare a very detailed (court) appeal against the order."
Israel has said the offices were part of the Palestinian self-rule Authority, which under the interim peace deals cannot operate in Jerusalem.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it, a move not recognised internationally, to claim all of the city as its capital.
Palestinians regard East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. The sides are due to negotiate the city's fate in talks due to run until May 1999.
